title: A lichen is two (or three)
teaches: A fungus farming algae, and how drying out and waking lets lichens live on bare rock
summary: **A lichen is a fungus with algae or cyanobacteria living inside it.** The fungus builds the body; the algae make sugar from light and feed it.
**Schwendener proposed this in 1867, and most lichen experts rejected it for a generation.** A single organism made of two seemed absurd.
**The fungus shapes the lichen.** Grown alone, a lichen fungus makes a shapeless lump; only with its partner does it take the lichen's form.
**Many lichens hold a third partner.** In 2016 Spribille and colleagues found yeasts of another fungus in the skin of lichens from six continents.
**About one named fungus in five lives as a lichen.** Most are sac fungi, partnered with green algae or with cyanobacteria.
**Lichens dry out to a few per cent water and wake within minutes of wetting.** Dry, they do nothing and lose nothing; they grow only while wet.
**Timing matters.** A lichen wet for long in good light gains; one wet only at night loses, because it breathes without making sugar.
**Lichens live where plants cannot.** On bare rock, bark, desert crust and Arctic tundra they are often the first life, slowly starting soil.

blocks.text: Old stone walls and gravestones are spotted with flat crusts of yellow, orange, grey and green, some in neat rings a hand across. Tree trunks in clean air carry leafy grey-green flakes and beards of grey threads. These are **lichens**. They grow on bare rock and bark, on fence posts and roof tiles, on Arctic tundra and desert soil, in places too dry, too cold or too poor for any plant.

For most of history they were filed as plants, a little like mosses. They have no roots, no leaves and no flowers, but they are green or coloured, and they seem to live on light and air. Under the microscope in the nineteenth century, a slice through one showed something odd: a body built of fungal threads, with a layer of small green cells tucked inside.

The lichen experts of the time took the green cells to be part of the lichen, its own organs for making food, and called them gonidia, a word for green reproductive cells. In 1867 the Swiss botanist Simon Schwendener argued that they were nothing of the kind. They were algae, living things in their own right, of kinds that also lived free on wet bark and stone. The threads around them were a fungus. A lichen, he wrote, in an image of his time, was a fungus that had captured algae and lived off them, as a master off his slaves.

Most lichenologists were outraged. To them a lichen was plainly one organism, with its own shape and its own name, and the idea that it was two was an insult to their life's work. The Finnish lichenologist William Nylander, the most eminent of them, ridiculed the theory and fought it to the end of his life.[^nylander] But evidence gathered. In the 1870s botanists sowed lichen fungus spores beside free-living algae and watched the threads seize the algal cells and start to build a lichen. In 1877 Albert Frank, whose root fungi appear in lesson 9, coined a new word for two different organisms living as one, and two years later Anton de Bary gave it the form that stuck: **symbiosis**, living together.

The fungus makes up most of a lichen's bulk and gives it its form. Grown alone in a dish, a lichen fungus makes only a slow, shapeless lump. With its partner it builds a body in layers: a tough skin of tightly packed threads on top, a thin layer of algae just beneath where the light reaches, a loose core of threads that holds air and water, and threads underneath that grip the surface.

blocks.caption: A slice through a leafy lichen, greatly magnified. The fungus builds every layer; the algae sit in a band just under the skin, where light reaches them.

blocks.text: The algae feed the fungus with the sugar they make from light. In return the algae get shelter from drying and strong sun, and the water and minerals the fungus soaks up from rain and dust. Many lichens pair with green algae; others, about one in ten, with cyanobacteria, blue-green bacteria that photosynthesise like algae and can also take nitrogen from the air and so fertilise the lichen and, in the end, the ground around it.[^nostoc] Whether this is a fair trade is still argued. The algae in a lichen grow more slowly than they would alone, and the fungus controls how many there are.

About a fifth of all named fungi live this way, nearly all of them sac fungi, and roughly twenty thousand kinds of lichen are known. Lichenized fungi arose several separate times, and some lineages later gave the habit up and went back to rotting wood or bark.

In Montana, two beard lichens hang from the same conifers. One, *Bryoria fremontii*, is dark brown; the other, *Bryoria tortuosa*, is yellowish and contains a poison, vulpinic acid. For a century they were treated as separate species, but when Toby Spribille and his colleagues read their genes in the 2010s they found the main fungus and the alga to be the same in both. So why did they differ?

Searching for genes that were active in one lichen but not the other, they found a third organism: a yeast, a single-celled club fungus, living in the lichen's skin. It was far commoner in the yellow lichen than in the brown. When they looked further, the same group of yeasts turned up in the skin of lichens from six continents. Their 2016 paper, which found the yeasts in dozens of lichen species, showed that many familiar lichens are at least three partners, two fungi and an alga, and that a century and a half of microscopes had missed one of them, embedded in the skin.[^three]

A lichen cannot keep water in. Its skin has no waxy coat and it has no roots to draw on, so it dries out with the air around it, in hours, to a few per cent water. It then stops: no growth, no breathing, nothing. Most living things die if they dry like that. A lichen waits. When dew or rain wets it again, it soaks up water in seconds, and within minutes its algae are making sugar again. Some have revived after many months kept dry. In 2005 the European Space Agency put two lichens outside a satellite, exposed to vacuum and cosmic radiation for over two weeks; back on Earth they took up water and were soon photosynthesising.

Being wet costs as well as earns. A wet lichen breathes, burning sugar, all the time it is wet; its algae make sugar only while there is light. So it matters when the water comes. A shower at night wakes the lichen in the dark, where it can only spend. Dew that forms before dawn and lasts into the morning is its best chance.

blocks.text: This is why lichens grow so slowly. Many crust lichens on rock widen by a millimetre or less a year, and some grow far more slowly still, a few hundredths of a millimetre a year, so a crust a few centimetres across on an old gravestone can be centuries old. It is also why they live where they do. On bare rock in a desert or the Arctic, where any plant would die between rains, a lichen just switches off.

Lichens are among the first life on new rock, on lava, on cliffs bared by a retreating glacier. They grip the rock and seep acids that loosen grains of its surface, and their own dead parts mix in, so that over centuries a thin skin of soil begins where mosses and then plants can follow. In the far north, reindeer lichens carpet the ground for hundreds of kilometres and are the main winter food of caribou and reindeer, which dig through the snow to reach them.

They also make chemicals found nowhere else, more than a thousand of them, many bitter or poisonous, which seem to deter grazers and screen strong sun. People used some as dyes for centuries: the old brown and purple dyes of Scottish tweed came from rock lichens, and so does litmus, the dye in the paper that turns red in acid and blue in alkali.[^litmus] And because lichens soak up whatever falls on them in rain, their chemistry reflects what is in the air. The lichen lessons that branch off after this one follow them out of and back into cities.

blocks.caption: Five questions on lichens
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

choices: A fungus with algae or cyanobacteria living inside it
A plant with a fungal disease
items.why: Schwendener showed the green cells are algae, and the threads around them a fungus. The fungus builds the body; its partners make sugar from light.

items.ask: Why did most lichenologists reject Schwendener's idea?
choices: A lichen looked plainly like a single organism with its own form
He could not show any green cells in lichens
It was proposed before microscopes existed
items.why: Lichens have a fixed shape and were named as species, so the idea that each was two organisms seemed absurd to them until sowing experiments proved it.

items.ask: What did Spribille and colleagues find in 2016?
choices: A third partner, yeasts of a second fungus, in the skin of many lichens
That lichens are a kind of plant after all
items.why: A third partner, a single-celled club fungus, was found in the skin of lichens from six continents, and more of it in the yellow beard lichen than the brown.

items.ask: A lichen is wet for four hours every night and dry all day. What happens to it?
choices: It slowly loses carbon, because it breathes in the dark and cannot make sugar
It grows fast, because it never dries in the sun
Nothing, because lichens do not breathe
items.why: A wet lichen burns sugar whenever it is wet, but its algae make sugar only in light. Wet only in darkness, it spends without earning.

items.ask: Why can lichens live on bare desert rock where plants die?
choices: They can dry out to a few per cent water and revive within minutes of wetting
They drink water from inside the rock
They make their own water from sugar
items.why: Drying out kills most plants. A lichen simply stops, losing nothing, and starts again when dew or rain wets it.

nylander.title: Nylander's war
nylander.text: Nylander described thousands of lichens and introduced chemical spot tests to tell them apart, tests still used today. He never accepted Schwendener's theory, and for some years after his death in 1899 a few followers held out with him.

nostoc.title: Nitrogen from the air
nostoc.text: Cyanobacteria such as *Nostoc* turn nitrogen gas into ammonia, a form living things can use. In wet old forests, lichens with cyanobacteria add a measurable amount of nitrogen to the forest floor as they fall and rot; a later lichen lesson follows this in the canopy.

three.title: How it was missed
three.text: The yeast cells sit in the outer skin, wrapped in the same material as the threads, and look under the microscope like part of the main fungus. Only genes, which spelled out a different fungus, gave them away. What the yeast does for the lichen, if anything, is still unknown.

litmus.title: Litmus
litmus.text: Litmus is extracted from lichens of the genus *Roccella*, which grow on sea cliffs in the Mediterranean and elsewhere. The dye was used as a purple colouring for cloth long before chemists used it to test acids.
